concepts.name: Functions of capital: market vs book value
concepts.definition: Capital absorbs unexpected losses, protects uninsured creditors, the deposit insurance fund and taxpayers, and funds investment. Economists use market value (net worth); accountants use book value; regulators use tiers. Market value shows solvency accurately, but book value gives banks discretion over when losses are recognised.
misconceptions: Thinking book value always reflects losses immediately

questions.prompt: How does an economist define an FI's capital?
options: Net worth: the market value of assets minus the market value of liabilities
The historical cost of assets minus liabilities
questions.explanation: This matches market value accounting.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a function of capital listed in the lecture?
options: Guaranteeing every depositor is paid in full
questions.explanation: Capital absorbs losses up to its size; it can't guarantee everyone.

questions.prompt: On a market value balance sheet, the value of an FI's loans falls. What happens to its net worth?
questions.explanation: Net worth = assets − liabilities; lower asset values cut it dollar for dollar.

questions.prompt: An FI has $70m securities and $30m loans, funded by $85m deposits. Loans fall in market value to $10m. What is its net worth?
questions.explanation: Assets 70 + 10 = 80; net worth = 80 − 85 = −$5m. Owners are wiped out.
feedback: That's the book value with a $5m provision.

questions.prompt: In the same example, without deposit insurance, what share of their deposits would depositors recover if the FI were liquidated?
questions.explanation: $80m of assets against $85m of deposits.

questions.prompt: Why might the FI's book value balance sheet look unchanged after that loss?
options: Book value accounting gives FIs discretion over how and when they recognise loan losses
Book value always equals market value
Deposits fall by the same amount
questions.explanation: It might only record, say, a $5m loan loss provision instead of the full $20m fall.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a reason given for not using market values for all assets?
options: Market values are always lower than book values
Hard to implement for institutions with many non-traded assets
It adds unnecessary variability to earnings
FIs become less willing to take long-term exposures
questions.explanation: Market values can be higher or lower than book values.

questions.prompt: Same FI ($70m securities, $30m loans, $85m deposits). Loans fall to $18m instead. What happens?
options: Net worth falls to $3m: capital absorbs the whole $12m loss and the FI stays solvent
questions.explanation: 88 − 85 = $3m: the $15m of capital is big enough to absorb a $12m loss.

concepts.name: Basel I and Basel II
concepts.definition: The Basel Committee (formed 1974, G-10) sets the global capital framework to level the playing field. Basel I: risk-weighted assets, credit risk only, Tier 1 ≥ 4%, total capital ≥ 8%. Basel II: three pillars (minimum capital, supervisory review, disclosure), standardised or IRB credit risk, plus operational risk. The GFC showed Basel II neglected liquidity and underestimated market risk.

questions.prompt: Why was the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision formed?
options: To strengthen the international banking system while making sure capital rules don't create competitive inequality: a level playing field
questions.explanation: National regulators (e.g. APRA) still set the actual ratios within the Basel framework.

questions.prompt: Under Basel I, what were the minimum Tier 1 and total capital ratios?
questions.explanation: Both measured against risk-weighted assets.

questions.prompt: Which risk did Basel I primarily recognise in risk-weighted assets?
questions.explanation: Market and operational risk came later.

questions.prompt: What is Pillar 2 of Basel II?
options: Supervisory review of each bank's internal process for assessing its capital adequacy
questions.explanation: Pillar 1 = minimum capital; Pillar 3 = disclosure.

questions.prompt: What two options did Basel II give banks for measuring credit risk?
options: The standardised approach and the internal ratings-based (IRB) approach
questions.explanation: IRB lets banks use their own rating systems, subject to approval.

questions.prompt: What weaknesses of Basel II did the GFC reveal?
options: Too little focus on liquidity, and market risk models that badly underestimated market risk
questions.explanation: Banks could have adequate capital but too few liquid assets.

questions.prompt: Which Basel II pillar does publishing a bank's risk exposures and capital structure belong to, and why?
options: Pillar 3: disclosure lets market participants assess the bank, adding market discipline
Pillar 1, because it sets minimum capital
None: disclosure isn't part of Basel
questions.explanation: Pillar 3 uses transparency as a lever for market discipline.

concepts.name: Basel III capital improvements
concepts.definition: Basel III (2010, phased in 2013–2019) splits Tier 1 into CET1 and AT1, adds LCR and NSFR, a non-risk-based leverage ratio (3% minimum) as a backstop, a 2.5% CET1 capital conservation buffer (CET1 + buffer = 7%), a countercyclical buffer of up to 2.5% CET1, and SIFI surcharges.
misconceptions: Thinking the leverage ratio is risk-weighted

questions.prompt: What does the capital conservation buffer require?
options: An extra 2.5% of RWAs held as CET1, which banks can draw on in stress
questions.explanation: CET1 minimum plus the buffer = 7% of RWAs.

questions.prompt: When may national authorities impose the countercyclical buffer?
options: When system-wide risk is building up, e.g. during rapid credit growth
questions.explanation: Up to 2.5% of RWAs, entirely CET1.

questions.prompt: What is the Tier 1 leverage ratio's role under Basel III?
options: A simple, non-risk-based backstop: Tier 1 capital ÷ total exposure, minimum 3%
questions.explanation: It catches banks whose risk weights understate their exposure.

questions.prompt: A bank's CET1 ratio falls to 6.5%. What happens under Basel III?
options: Constraints on its capital distributions (e.g. dividends) apply, because it's below the 7% minimum-plus-buffer
questions.explanation: Below 7% CET1, supervisors restrict distributions.

questions.prompt: How does Basel III's Pillar 2 address compensation?
options: Pay should be sensitive to risk outcomes over several years, e.g. deferred bonuses and clawbacks
questions.explanation: Clawbacks reduce or reverse pay if exposures later go bad.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a Basel III improvement listed in the lecture?
options: Splitting Tier 1 into CET1 and AT1
questions.explanation: Requirements remain risk-based, with the leverage ratio as a backstop.

questions.prompt: Basel III also introduced this leverage ratio. What goes in the denominator?
options: Total on- and off-balance-sheet exposure, with no risk weighting
questions.explanation: It's deliberately simple and non-risk-based.
questions.equation: \text{Tier 1 leverage ratio} = \frac{\text{Tier 1 capital}}{\text{Total exposure (on- and off-balance-sheet)}}

questions.prompt: A bank's CET1 minimum is 4.5% of RWAs. With the full conservation and countercyclical buffers, what CET1 ratio does it need to avoid restrictions?
questions.explanation: 4.5% + 2.5% conservation + 2.5% countercyclical = 9.5%.
feedback: That leaves out the countercyclical buffer.

questions.prompt: Australia is phasing out which capital instrument, a first among OECD countries?
questions.explanation: Listed among the developments and criticisms of risk-based capital.

concepts.name: Credit risk-weighted assets (standardised approach)
concepts.definition: On-balance-sheet assets get risk weights by category: 0%, 20%, 50%, 100% or 150%. Off-balance-sheet items are first converted to credit equivalent amounts (face value × conversion factor; for derivatives, potential exposure plus current exposure), then risk-weighted.
misconceptions: Applying risk weights to the face value of off-balance-sheet items

questions.prompt: Which risk weight applies to cash and Treasury securities?
questions.explanation: Category 1 assets are treated as risk-free.

questions.prompt: Under the standardised approach, what risk weight applies to most commercial (C&I) loans?
questions.explanation: Category 4 includes unrated C&I loans and corporate loans rated BBB+ to BB−.

questions.prompt: Why are off-balance-sheet items converted to 'credit equivalent amounts'?
options: They're contingent claims, so capital is held against the on-balance-sheet credit risk they could create, not their face value
questions.explanation: The credit equivalent amount is then risk-weighted like an on-balance-sheet item.

questions.prompt: A bank shifts $100m from commercial loans (100% weight) into Treasury bills (0%). What happens to its risk-weighted assets?
questions.explanation: RWA falls by $100m, raising its risk-based capital ratios.

questions.prompt: A $80m two-year loan commitment has a 50% conversion factor and 100% risk weight. What does it add to RWA?
questions.explanation: Credit equivalent = 80 × 0.5 = 40; × 100% = $40m.

questions.prompt: A $50m commercial letter of credit has a 20% conversion factor and 100% risk weight. What does it add to RWA?
A 4-year interest rate swap has notional $100m, a 0.5% conversion factor and a current replacement cost of $3m. What's its credit equivalent amount?
questions.explanation: Potential exposure 100 × 0.5% = 0.5, plus current exposure 3 = $3.5m.

questions.prompt: A 2-year FX forward has notional $40m, a 5% conversion factor and a replacement cost of −$1m. What's its credit equivalent amount?
questions.explanation: Potential 40 × 5% = 2; current exposure is max(−1, 0) = 0; total $2m.
feedback: That subtracts the negative replacement cost.

questions.prompt: A bank holds $100m cash (0%), $50m interbank deposits (20%), $200m residential mortgages (50%), $300m business loans (100%) and $20m of loans rated below B− (150%). What are its credit RWAs?
feedback: That weights the last item at 0%.

concepts.name: Calculating capital ratios
concepts.definition: CET1 ratio = CET1 ÷ RWA; Tier 1 ratio = (CET1 + AT1) ÷ RWA; total capital ratio = (Tier 1 + Tier 2) ÷ RWA; leverage ratio = Tier 1 ÷ total exposure. The risk-based ratio usually exceeds the leverage ratio when many assets have weights below 100%.
misconceptions: Dividing the leverage ratio by RWA

questions.prompt: A bank's risk-weighted assets rise while its capital is unchanged. What happens to its total capital ratio?
questions.explanation: RWA is the denominator, so the ratio falls.
feedback: A bigger denominator lowers the ratio.
questions.equation: \text{Total capital ratio} = \frac{\text{Tier 1 capital} + \text{Tier 2 capital}}{\text{Total risk-weighted assets}}

questions.prompt: Which capital goes into the CET1 ratio's numerator?
options: Common equity Tier 1: common stock and retained earnings
questions.explanation: In the lecture example: $40m retained earnings + $30m common stock = $70m CET1.

questions.prompt: Tier 1 capital is $100,000. Assets are $1m with a 0% weight and $1m with a 100% weight. What are the Tier 1 risk-based and leverage ratios?
In the lecture's Table 20-9 example, CET1 = $70m, AT1 = $10m and RWA = $830m. What is the Tier 1 capital ratio?
National Bank: deposits $960m, common stock $45m, retained earnings $40m, subordinated debentures $25m; RWA = $730m. What is its total risk-based capital ratio?
questions.explanation: (45 + 40 + 25) ÷ 730 = 15.07%. Subordinated debt is Tier 2.

questions.prompt: Table 20-9: Tier 1 = $80m, Tier 2 = $35m, RWA = $830m. What is the total capital ratio?
questions.explanation: (80 + 35) ÷ 830 = 13.86%. Slide 35 prints 13.68%, which looks like a typo: the arithmetic gives 13.86%.
feedback: That's the figure printed on the slide, but (80 + 35) ÷ 830 = 13.86%.

questions.prompt: National Bank has total assets of $1,090m, CET1 of $85m and RWA of $730m. Why is its leverage ratio (7.80%) lower than its CET1 ratio (11.64%)?
options: The leverage ratio divides by all $1,090m of assets, while risk weighting shrinks RWA to $730m (cash, T-bills at 0%, mortgages at 50%)
Because the leverage ratio uses market values
Because RWA is larger than total assets
questions.explanation: When many assets have weights under 100%, the risk-based ratio exceeds the leverage ratio.

questions.prompt: A bank with $30m Tier 1 capital has $440m RWA. Does it meet Basel I's 8% total capital minimum if it has no Tier 2 capital?
options: Yes: 6.82% is above 4%, so it passes everything
questions.explanation: It meets the 4% Tier 1 minimum but not the 8% total.

concepts.name: Criticisms of risk-based capital ratios
concepts.definition: Risk weights may not reflect true risk, rely on credit ratings, largely ignore portfolio diversification and concentration, and Basel III adds costly complexity.
misconceptions: Thinking risk weights capture concentration risk

questions.prompt: Which is a criticism of risk-based capital ratios listed in the lecture?
options: They largely ignore credit portfolio diversification and concentration risk
They don't use credit ratings at all
They apply only to small banks
questions.explanation: Each loan is weighted on its own, so correlation isn't captured.

questions.prompt: Why are risk weights based on credit ratings criticised?
options: Ratings can be wrong or slow to change, so weights may not match true risk
questions.explanation: This is part of the 'validity of risk weights' concern.

questions.prompt: Two banks each hold $500m of 100%-weighted loans. Bank A lends to one industry; Bank B to ten unrelated industries. How do their risk-based capital requirements compare?
options: They're the same, even though Bank A has far more concentration risk: the criticism the lecture raises
Bank A must hold more capital
Bank B must hold more capital
questions.explanation: Risk weights ignore diversification and concentration, linking back to Week 7's MPT ideas.
feedback: Standardised weights don't add for concentration.
